one_liner: Rust WebAssembly interpreter with near-zero startup through lazy translation; its v2 engine also out-executes WAMR, Wasm3 and Pulley interpreters.
what_it_does: Embeddable Wasm interpreter (crate `wasmi`, plus `wasmi_wasi` for WASI preview 1, a `wasmi` CLI and an official Wasm C-API built with CMake into libwasmi.a/.so) that loosely mirrors the Wasmtime API (Engine, Store, Linker, Module, Instance), so many Wasmtime hosts can switch with small edits. It runs no_std, supports fuel metering, a deterministic profile and Wasm 2.0 plus tail calls, multi-memory, memory64, SIMD and relaxed SIMD (GC, function references, threads and exception handling are not supported). Modules can be compiled eagerly, lazily translated after eager validation (the default) or fully lazily.
how_it_is_fast: Startup: with CompilationMode::LazyTranslation (default) or Lazy, Module::new only parses and validates (or, in Lazy mode, does not even validate) function bodies, and each function is translated to Wasmi bytecode on first call, so instantiating a huge module that runs few functions costs almost nothing; translation is linear-time ('JIT bomb resisting'). Execution: Wasmi v2 has a new IR whose operators write results into accumulator registers (the design used by Wasm3 and Stitch), fixed 64-bit cells, operator fusion (compare+branch and similar), tail-call-based operator dispatch where LLVM guarantees tail calls (auto-dispatch, falling back to a loop), a lock-free append-only code map and cached instance data; the changelog reports v2 about 2.2x faster than v1 geomean.
when_to_use: Hosts that instantiate many short-lived or large modules and call only a few functions (plugins, smart contracts, per-request sandboxes): lazy Wasmi v2 instantiated the 7-module startup suite at x1.37 of the per-case optimum on EPYC 7763, against x33.27 for V8 and x1634.19 for Wasmtime Cranelift.

Platforms where native code generation is forbidden or unavailable (iOS, W^X, embedded, no_std) and you still want a fast interpreter: v2 eager executed at x12.40 on EPYC 7763, x8.06 on Apple M4 Pro and x8.36 on Xeon Platinum 8573C, ahead of WAMR fast-interp (x17.07/x18.64/x12.43), Wasm3 eager (x16.51/x10.71/x11.95) and Wasmtime Pulley (x27.92/x23.97/x23.70).
Rust hosts that need deterministic execution or fuel metering (blockchains such as Soroban and smoldot): fuel is tied to the input Wasm bytecode and costs are configurable in v2.
Projects that want a Wasmtime-shaped API without Cranelift's binary size and compile latency, or a C/C++ host that can link a Rust-built static library through the Wasm C-API.
when_not_to_use: Compute-bound long-running guests: Wasmtime Cranelift (x1.15) and V8 (x1.05) executed about 10x faster than Wasmi v2 (x12.40) on EPYC 7763, and even Wasmer Singlepass (x2.95) and Wasmtime Winch (x2.35) were about 4-5x faster.
When the fastest interpreter matters most: Silverfir-nano's interpreter was ahead on every measured CPU (x9.02 vs x12.40 on EPYC 7763, x5.97 vs x8.06 on M4 Pro, x7.01 vs x8.36 on Xeon 8573C).
Guests that need Wasm GC, typed function references, threads or exception handling (all only tracked, not implemented), or WASI preview 2/components.

Untrusted modules in fully Lazy mode where results must match other engines: the API docs say Lazy 'must not be used if the result of Wasm execution must be deterministic amongst multiple Wasm implementations', since invalid function bodies are only rejected when first called.

Debug builds: the usage guide says an unoptimized Wasmi can be 100x slower, and because the executor is generic over Store<T> it is compiled in your crate, so your own profile needs lto = "fat" and codegen-units = 1.

integration.form: crate (wasmi); C-API static/shared library via CMake (crates/c_api); CLI (wasmi)
integration.dependencies: pure Rust: wasmparser, spin, internal wasmi_* crates; optional wat; the C-API build needs CMake and a Rust toolchain
integration.platforms: any Rust target including no_std; tail-call dispatch only on targets with guaranteed LLVM tail calls in optimized builds, portable loop dispatch elsewhere
integration.thread_safety: Engine is cloneable and shared; Store is Send and Sync (changelog, PR #566); one Store executes on one thread at a time; the Wasm threads proposal is not supported.
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial — the API loosely mirrors Wasmtime's (Engine/Store/Linker/Module), but it is a different crate with a narrower feature set (no components, GC, threads or exception handling)

gotchas: The startup headline compares deferred work with eager work: the harness times only Module::new plus instantiate and never calls into the module, so in lazy modes no function body is translated (and in Lazy mode none is validated) inside the timed region, while Cranelift, Winch and V8 compile everything. The per-case 'optimal runtime' is mostly Wasmi v2 (lazy, unchecked) itself (x1.04), which uses the unsafe Module::new_unchecked. Fairer numbers on EPYC 7763: default lazy-translation x10.66 and eager x38.88, the latter slower than V8 (x33.27) there and on M4 Pro (x25.69 vs x21.11) but faster on Xeon 8573C (x22.62 vs x29.21).

Benchmark builds are not the defaults: the suite builds Wasmi v2 with default-features = false and only auto-dispatch and validate (no std and no memory64, which the changelog says 'may improve execution performance'), and Wasmtime with default-features = false (runtime, anyhow, plus the chosen backend), so Cranelift compiles without its default parallel-compilation feature, single-threaded; a stock Wasmtime would start faster on a multi-core host. The plots record no Wasmi beta, baseline versions or rustc version (the README links v2.0.0-beta.7, Cargo.toml pins 2.0.0-beta.10).

The v2 engine is young: the 2.0 betas fixed several translation bugs (multi-value br_table, fused fabs+fneg, SIMD load accumulator handling, isub immediate lowering, a memory-invalidation bug when tail-calling host functions), and the extra-checks feature, which guards against undefined behaviour if translation invariants break, is off by default (up to 20% cost when on).

Security history: a critical out-of-bounds write for host-to-Wasm calls with more than 128 parameters (GHSA-75jp-vq8x-h4cq, 2024-03) and a high-severity linear-memory use-after-free (GHSA-g4v2-cjqp-rfmq, 2025-12); the README lists two audits (SRLabs for 0.31.0, Runtime Verification for 0.36-0.38), none of the v2 engine.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick Wasmi over WAMR, Wasm3 or Stitch when you want the fastest instantiation plus a top-tier interpreter in safe-to-embed Rust with fuel metering and a Wasmtime-like API (it beat all three on execution geomean on EPYC 7763, M4 Pro and Xeon 8573C); pick Silverfir-nano's interpreter instead only if raw interpreter throughput matters more than startup and maturity, and WAMR when you need a C code base with optional AOT/JIT tiers.
verified_claims_summary: In the author's own wasmi-benchmarks suite (criterion, 10 samples, 2 s measurement, fat-LTO bench profile, unpinned stable Rust) plotted for an AMD EPYC 7763, the startup geomean (Module::new plus instantiate of 7 modules, relative to the fastest runtime per case) was x1.37 for lazy Wasmi v2, x10.66 lazy-translation, x38.88 eager, against x33.27 V8, x298.15 Wasmtime Winch and x1634.19 Wasmtime Cranelift; the execution geomean over 21 cases (instance set up outside the timed loop, several cases assert their outputs) was x12.40 for eager Wasmi v2 against x17.07 WAMR fast-interp, x16.51 Wasm3, x27.92 Pulley and x1.15 Cranelift. I re-read these labels from the SVGs and also read the M4 Pro and Xeon 8573C plots, where Wasmi v2 keeps its interpreter ranking (x8.06 and x8.36).
status_note: Actively maintained by its author with Stellar Development Foundation sponsorship; v2.0.0 released 2026-09-01 under Apache-2.0 OR MIT, used by Soroban, Typst, Zellij and smoldot, and copyable as a crate or C library today.
